title: Complete disjoint NP pairs
formal:
Let \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), and let
\[
\mathcal D=\{(A,B):A,B\subseteq\Sigma^{*},\ A,B\in\mathrm{NP},\ A\cap B=\varnothing\}.
\]
Does there exist a disjoint NP pair that is complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions of pairs? Precisely, is
\[
\exists(A,B)\in\mathcal D\ \forall(C,D)\in\mathcal D\ \exists f\in\mathrm{FP}\
\forall x\in\Sigma^{*}\
\bigl[(x\in C\Rightarrow f(x)\in A)\land(x\in D\Rightarrow f(x)\in B)\bigr]
\]
true? Here \(\mathrm{FP}\) consists of total polynomial-time functions \(\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}\), as specified below. The target pair is fixed before the source pair is chosen; the reduction and its polynomial running-time bound may depend on the source pair.
definitions:
\(\Sigma^{*}\) is the set of all finite binary strings, including the empty string, and \(|x|\) denotes the number of bits of \(x\). A language is an arbitrary subset of \(\Sigma^{*}\). The pairs are ordered, and disjointness means that no string belongs to both components. Empty component languages are permitted. The quantifiers range over all pairs that are actually disjoint, without requiring their disjointness to be provable in any particular theory.

Computations use uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite control, a fixed finite number of tapes per machine, and tape alphabet \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), where \(\square\) is blank. Each tape has cells indexed by nonnegative integers and one head, initially at cell zero; a left move at cell zero leaves the head there. There is one read-only input tape and finitely many initially blank work tapes. One transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the finite state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape, and moves each head by at most one cell. A transducer additionally has an initially empty output string and may append at most one output bit per transition. Each transition costs one step. Verifiers halt in an accept or reject state; transducers halt with their accumulated binary output. The finite program and tape count are independent of input length. There is no advice, random input or oracle access.

A language \(L\) belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there exist such a verifier \(V\), integers \(a,b\ge1\) and \(k,\ell\ge0\), with the following properties. For every \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\), the verifier on input \(x\#y\) halts within \(b(|x|+|y|+2)^{\ell}\) steps, and for every \(x\in\Sigma^{*}\),
\[
x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists y\in\Sigma^{*}\ \bigl(|y|\le a(|x|+1)^{k}\ \land\ V(x\#y)\text{ accepts}\bigr).
\]
The string \(y\) is a certificate. These verifier and polynomial constants may depend on \(L\), but not on \(x\) or \(y\).

A function \(f:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{FP}\) if there exist one deterministic transducer \(M\), an integer \(c\ge1\) and an integer \(d\ge0\) such that, for every \(x\in\Sigma^{*}\), \(M\) on input \(x\) halts within \(c(|x|+1)^{d}\) steps and outputs \(f(x)\). Thus \(f\) is defined and polynomial-time computable on every binary input, including strings outside the source promise. Its output length is charged through bit writing and is consequently polynomially bounded.

A reduction from \((C,D)\) to \((A,B)\) is one such function \(f\) satisfying both displayed implications. The same function handles both sides. For \(x\notin C\cup D\), its output may lie anywhere in \(\Sigma^{*}\), including inside \(A\cup B\), but the same totality and time bound still apply. Neither surjectivity nor reverse membership implications are required. For a fixed source pair the transducer, coefficient and degree must work for every input length; they need not be shared by different source pairs. The target does not require a computable procedure that takes descriptions of source pairs and produces their reductions.

The mathematical target concerns the ordinary, unrelativized classes \(\mathrm{NP}\) and \(\mathrm{FP}\). Completeness for a restricted family of pairs, or completeness or noncompleteness after supplying machines with an oracle, is a different assertion.

context_blocks.text: Pudlák's 2017 revision defines precisely these pair reductions and conjectures that no complete disjoint NP pair exists. The card preserves its yes-or-no existence question, so proving that conjecture gives a negative answer.

A propositional proof system is a polynomial-time map whose range is exactly the Boolean tautologies. A p-optimal system can translate proofs from every such system in polynomial time; its existence would imply a complete disjoint NP pair. Pudlák's Proposition 5.2 in fact obtains this implication from the weaker requirement that one system polynomially bounds the shortest proof lengths of every other system. No converse implication is asserted.

Dose's 2019 result constructs an oracle relative to which no complete disjoint NP pairs exist even though every NP language has a p-optimal proof system. The proof systems in that result concern NP languages, whereas the propositional implication concerns tautologies; the results do not contradict one another.

Egidy's ICALP 2026 paper constructs an oracle relative to which disjoint NP pairs have no complete pair and the polynomial-time hierarchy remains infinite. An oracle supplies membership answers for a fixed auxiliary language to the machines defining both the classes and reductions. This result concerns those modified classes and does not establish nonexistence for the ordinary classes on this card.

why: A complete pair would be a universal promise problem for two disjoint cases that each have efficiently checkable certificates. The question links the structure of promise problems to the possible existence of a strongest propositional proof system and to feasible versions of incompleteness.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition, including the target languages' NP membership and disjointness and the total polynomial-time reductions for every source pair, or a complete Lean proof of its full logical negation:
\[
\forall(A,B)\in\mathcal D\ \exists(C,D)\in\mathcal D\ \forall f\in\mathrm{FP}\
\exists x\in\Sigma^{*}\
\bigl[(x\in C\land f(x)\notin A)\lor(x\in D\land f(x)\notin B)\bigr].
\]
In the negative statement the witness source pair may depend on the candidate target pair but must defeat every eligible reduction; the witness string may depend on the reduction. All computational classes and reductions must have the definitions above. A conditional implication, an oracle construction, or failure of one candidate pair does not alone decide this unconditional target.

progress.text: Version 2 states the pair reduction, the implication from length-optimal proof systems, and the conjectured nonexistence of a complete pair.
The MFCS paper separates related conjectures by an oracle construction without deciding the unrelativized complete-pair question.
The ICALP paper gives a further oracle with no complete disjoint NP pairs; its corollary also keeps the relativized polynomial-time hierarchy infinite.
Checked source revisions and subsequent results; repaired malformed delimiters and made verifier bounds, total reductions, quantifier dependencies and the full negation explicit.

sentences: A disjoint NP pair consists of two nonoverlapping sets of binary strings, each with polynomially checkable certificates.
The question asks whether one such pair can receive every other pair through a single total deterministic polynomial-time function.
That function must map each source side to its corresponding target side, while its behavior outside the source promise is unrestricted apart from total polynomial time.
Pudlák conjectures nonexistence and relates the question to the strength of propositional proof systems.
The checked results through July 2026 include oracle separations but do not resolve the unrelativized existence target.

checked_sources: Read data/cards/TCS-7273.json and the current formulation/source rules. The existing target already allows arbitrary disjoint NP languages and one total polynomial-time function for both sides. Its definitions contain broken math delimiters around the binary-string function domain and codomain. No target, category, relation or importance change is proposed.

Checked the arXiv landing page for 1601.01487: v1 was submitted 7 January 2016 and v2 on 18 May 2017, with no later arXiv revision displayed on 16 September 2026. The downloaded v2 PDF has a 22 May 2017 title-page date. Read Section 5.1 p. 25: the function maps A into C and B into D, with no reverse or outside-promise clause. Conjecture DisjNP is the negative answer to the card. Proposition 5.2 uses length-optimal proof systems; footnote 14 distinguishes the earlier p-optimal result.

Checked publisher metadata for the journal version: Bulletin of Symbolic Logic 23(4), December 2017, pp. 405-441, DOI 10.1017/bsl.2017.32; Cambridge displays online publication 15 February 2018. An author-hosted later manuscript is dated 21 November 2017, but the draft's page locators and definition audit intentionally use the inspected arXiv v2. No claim is made that the arXiv pagination is the journal pagination.

Read Dose MFCS 2019 publisher PDF abstract and Sections 1-2, including Theorem 6 p. 47:5. It constructs an oracle with no complete DisjNP pairs while every NP language has a p-optimal proof system, and states additional UP/NP-intersection-coNP properties. This is an oracle theorem, not ordinary nonexistence. Its NP-language proof systems must not be confused with propositional proof systems for TAUT. The full construction proof was not independently verified.

Read Egidy ICALP 2026 publisher PDF Section 2 pp. 88:6-88:7: disjoint pairs over binary strings and one FP map preserving the two components, matching the retained definition. Read Proposition 31 and Theorem 32 p. 88:16 and Corollary 33 p. 88:17. All noncompleteness conclusions there are relative to a constructed oracle; Theorem 32 can extend a fixed background oracle, and Corollary 33 retains an infinite relativized PH. The paper's separate unrelativized results concern jump operators, not a resolution of ordinary DisjNP completeness. No full-proof audit is claimed.

Bounded later searches through 16 September 2026 used complete disjoint NP pairs, DisjNP, 2025/2026, and dates after 1 July 2026. The direct latest checked completeness result is the ICALP 2026 oracle theorem. Also inspected the abstract and Section 1.1 p.4 of Liu-Mazor-Pass, ECCC TR26-051, PDF dated 6 April 2026: its hard-disjoint-pair consequence has hardness and derandomization assumptions and concerns separation hardness, not completeness for all disjoint pairs. Inspected primary abstract of Ilango TR25-095, 15 July 2025: it uses an optimal-proof-system nonexistence assumption for a cryptographic construction, not a proof of that assumption. These nearby results do not settle this card.

NP certificate and runtime bounds are written as independent integer coefficient/exponent bounds; FP requires totality and a worst-case polynomial clock on all strings, including outside the promise. The reduction machine and its clock may depend on a source pair, but are fixed across all lengths. No effective selection of reductions from source descriptions, no disjointness-proof requirement in a fixed theory, no nonuniform advice and no oracle have been added. The negative quantifiers require a source pair fixed before all reductions, with a possibly different counterexample string for each reduction.
